title: Care for a foal from birth to weaning

lessons.title: The first days and weeks
lessons.html:
The first 24 hours

The first day decides much of a foal's future health. Check these milestones and record the times:

  • Stands within about 1 hour and suckles within about 2 hours.
  • Passes meconium (dark, sticky first dung) within a few hours. Straining without result needs the vet.
  • Passes urine within about 12 hours (colts may take a little longer).
  • The placenta is passed within about 3 hours and kept for the vet to check.

Dip the navel as recommended by the vet, and watch it for swelling or dampness in the following days. Many studs have the vet examine the foal and test its antibody (IgG) level at 12 to 24 hours to confirm it received enough colostrum.

Daily checks

  • Foal is bright, follows the mare and suckles often.
  • Mare's udder is soft, not tight and dripping.
  • Normal dung (soft but formed; mild "foal heat" diarrhoea around 7 to 12 days is common, but call the vet if the foal is dull, stops suckling or the diarrhoea is severe).
  • Joints not swollen, navel dry, breathing calm.
  • Legs straight; mild laxity often improves, but tell the vet about crooked legs early, as correction is time-sensitive.

Handling the young foal

Early, gentle handling makes later work safer.

  1. Move the foal with one arm around the chest and one around the hindquarters.
  2. Fit a foal slip (small headcollar) and teach the foal to accept it.
  3. Teach leading with a rump rope behind the hindquarters, alongside the mare.
  4. Pick up and handle each foot daily, rewarding calm behaviour.
  5. Keep sessions short. Never let the foal learn that nipping or kicking works.

Safety

Always keep the mare in sight of the foal and have a second handler for the mare. Many mares are protective and will kick or bite to defend their foal.

lessons.title: Growth, health programme and weaning
lessons.html:
Feeding the growing foal

  • Milk provides most nutrition in the first two months. From a few weeks old the foal starts nibbling grass, hay and the mare's feed.
  • From about 2 to 3 months, offer a balanced creep feed in a creep feeder that the mare cannot reach, so the foal gets enough protein, minerals and energy as the mare's milk declines.
  • Avoid overfeeding grain; fast growth spurts can cause bone and joint problems (developmental orthopaedic disease).
  • Fresh water and good-quality pasture or hay always.

Health programme

Plan with the vet and record everything:

AreaTypical approach
VaccinationStart the foal's course at the age the vet recommends, including African horse sickness as required
DewormingFoals are vulnerable to roundworms; use products and timing the vet and label recommend
Hoof careFarrier checks and trims every 4 to 6 weeks to keep feet balanced
Tick and fly controlProducts safe for foals, as labelled
Growth checksMonitor weight, height and leg conformation

Weaning

Foals are usually weaned at about 4 to 6 months, depending on the stud's system, the mare's condition and the foal's development.

Methods

  • Gradual (paddock) weaning: remove one or two mares at a time from a group, so foals stay with familiar companions. Lower stress.
  • Fence-line weaning: mare and foal in neighbouring paddocks with a safe fence, so they can see each other for a few days.
  • Abrupt weaning: mare and foal separated completely. Higher stress; only use in very safe facilities.

Good weaning practice

  1. Wean healthy foals that already eat creep feed well.
  2. Avoid weaning at the same time as vaccinations, transport or other stresses.
  3. Use safe paddocks with no wire or gaps, and stables without sharp edges.
  4. Reduce the mare's feed for a few days to help dry her off; check her udder.
  5. Watch weaned foals closely for injury, weight loss and illness.

Key points

  • Check standing, suckling, meconium and urine milestones in the first day.
  • A soft udder and a bright foal show good suckling.
  • Handle foals early and gently; keep the mare in sight.
  • Introduce creep feed at 2 to 3 months; avoid overfeeding grain.
  • Follow a vet-planned health programme and farrier care.
  • Wean at about 4 to 6 months using a low-stress method.
